Ever feel like you've made the same decision five times without actually deciding?

Option A feels right on Monday. Option B looks better on Tuesday. By Wednesday, you're researching everything again and wondering why you can't settle on an answer.

Sometimes it helps to look underneath the options. Decision Untangler is designed for that kind of reflection: https://decisionuntangler.garrettsdevdesk.com

Going back and forth on a decision doesn't always mean you need more information.

Sometimes you've already considered the practical details several times. Another round of research may bring you back to the same unanswered questions.

Try writing down what you genuinely don't know yet. If the list is short, the difficulty may have more to do with the tradeoffs than the available facts.

Two options can look equally reasonable on paper and still leave you feeling stuck.

Maybe the difficulty isn't figuring out which one has the better features, salary, location, or timeline. Maybe each option represents something important that you don't want to give up.

Try asking, "What does each choice represent to me?" That question can reveal more than another pros-and-cons list.

Choosing between two jobs might really mean weighing stability against possibility.

Moving somewhere new might bring up familiarity versus a fresh start. Starting a project might involve safety, curiosity, or the fear of missing an opportunity.

Try naming what each option represents before comparing the practical details again. Decision Untangler can help you explore those questions: https://decisionuntangler.garrettsdevdesk.com

A good decision can still come with a sense of loss.

You might be excited about a new opportunity while feeling sad about leaving something familiar. You might choose stability while wondering what could have happened if you'd taken a bigger risk.

Those feelings don't automatically mean you made the wrong choice. Sometimes they simply reflect that both possibilities mattered to you.

When you're stuck between two reasonable options, try changing the question.

Instead of asking which option is better, ask what you're actually choosing between. You may discover that the real tension involves values, priorities, or things you care about more deeply than you first realized.

Have you ever struggled with a decision because both options offered something you genuinely wanted?
